lesson.title: When Order and History Matter: The General Multiplication Rule
lesson.summary: The general multiplication rule, P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B given A), handles dependent events like sampling without replacement, where the first outcome changes the odds of the second.
lesson.body:
The multiplication rule from the previous chapter only works when two events are independent, but many of the most important situations in statistics involve events that clearly affect each other. The general multiplication rule handles both cases at once: P(A and B) = P(A) times P(B given A), where P(B given A) means the probability B happens once it is already known that A happened. When A and B are independent, learning that A happened does not change B's odds at all, so P(B given A) simply equals P(B), and the general rule collapses back into the simpler multiplication rule from before. The general rule is the more fundamental relationship, and last chapter's version was really just the special case where conditioning happens to change nothing.

The general rule becomes necessary the moment one event physically changes the conditions the second event unfolds under, which happens constantly when sampling without replacement. Draw a card from a deck and set it aside rather than putting it back, and the deck the second draw comes from is no longer the same fifty two card deck the first draw came from: it has one fewer card, and if the drawn card mattered to the event of interest, the composition has shifted in a way that directly changes the second event's probability.

Consider drawing two cards from a standard 52 card deck without replacement and asking for the probability both cards are aces. The first draw has probability 4/52 of being an ace, since 4 of the 52 cards are aces. Given that the first card drawn was an ace, only 3 aces remain among the 51 cards left in the deck, so the conditional probability the second draw is also an ace, given the first was, is 3/51. The general multiplication rule combines these: P(both aces) = P(first is an ace) times P(second is an ace given first is an ace) = 4/52 times 3/51. Multiplying numerators and denominators gives 12/2652, which simplifies to 1/221.

It is worth seeing explicitly why the independent events shortcut would fail here. Treating the two draws as independent and computing 4/52 times 4/52 would give 16/2704, which reduces to 1/169, a noticeably different and incorrect answer, because it wrongly assumes the deck still has 4 aces out of 52 cards on the second draw when in fact removing the first ace left only 3 aces among 51 cards. Sampling without replacement is dependent by its very nature, and the general multiplication rule is what correctly captures that.

This chapter has been using the conditional probability P(B given A) as an input that simply had to be figured out from context, such as counting the 3 remaining aces among 51 remaining cards by hand. The next chapter turns that idea around, giving conditional probability its own precise formula, one that can be applied to any two events as long as their individual and joint probabilities are already known, rather than relying on being able to recount a shrinking deck by hand every time.
